SEC14A-01.note: Inverted order: subject is 'two silver pennies', placed after a long participial interruption; plural, past (1911 narrative) -> 'were tucked'. 'was tucked' is strongest, pulled by singular 'slab'/'floor'/'parchment' before the blank. Tense options need context to reject.

SEC14A-02.note: Main verb needed for singular head 'practice' after a long modifier full of plurals (quotations, editors, dictionaries, sources) -> 'has given'. 'have given' strongest (attraction). '-ing' option rejectable by the general 'gerund is rarely the main-verb key' habit.
SEC14A-02.phase2_note: Ship, but not on the same form as SEC14B-01 (shared template).

SEC14A-03.note: 'four separate pieces of information' announces a list of noun phrases -> colon. Semicolon fails (list is not an independent clause), period leaves a fragment; ', which the direction...' is plainly ungrammatical and falls without parsing.

SEC14A-04.note: Correlative 'so high a multiple ... that' takes no punctuation before 'that'. ', so that' is strongest (looks like a result clause but duplicates the earlier 'so'). Comma and colon before 'that' fall to the general 'no mark before that' rule without parsing.

SEC14A-05.note: 'Whatever he wrote ... has seldom survived' is a new independent clause with a noun-clause subject; the verb 'has' is far from the blank. Comma (A) is a splice disguised as 'called a cue, whatever...'; strongest. ', that whatever' is malformed on sight.

SEC14A-06.note: 'the boards ... facing a choice' has no finite verb, so it must be the object of a participle: ', leaving the'. Period, 'although' and 'whereupon' all leave verbless clauses. Strongest: period (A), since 'facing' is six words away and easily misread as finite.

SEC14B-01.note: Subject is the noun clause 'Whether those spores survive...' (singular) and 'since the 1980s' demands present perfect -> 'has kept'. 'have kept' strongest (plural attractors voles, squirrels, truffles). 'since' sits seven words after the blank, so tense needs reading.
SEC14B-01.phase2_note: Ship, but not on the same form as SEC14A-02: same template and same 'singular has + pp' key.

SEC14B-02.note: Pronoun is the object of 'considered' (considered him too careless) -> whom; the belief ended with the 1998 find ('until'), so simple past, not present perfect. Strongest: C (right case, wrong tense) and D (right tense, 'who' feels natural before 'cavers').

SEC14B-03.note: Dangling modifier: 'Bleached nearly white...' must attach to the lichen, so the lichen is the subject -> D. A is strongest: 'the lichen's' starts the clause but the possessive makes 'collector' the subject. Standard SAT modifier template.

SEC14B-04.note: Two independent clauses ('they are all but undetectable' / 'the concentration ... climbs') -> semicolon. A and C are comma splices (C also misattaches 'after sunset'); C is strongest. ', which the concentration' is ungrammatical on sight.

SEC14B-05.note: Introductory 'While' clause needs a comma before the main clause 'a seed crystal ... grows'; without it 'cools a seed crystal' garden-paths into a transitive misreading (B, strongest). Period leaves a fragment; ', and' after a subordinate clause is a known-wrong form.

SEC14B-06.note: Appositive 'a cyanobacterium whose cells measure ... and slip ...' is closed by the comma before 'accounts'; 'whose' supplies the needed relative. D (comma) is strongest, tempting by symmetry with the comma after Prochlorococcus. Semicolon/period mid-appositive fall on sight.

tells: Added-connector distractors are never keyed in the boundary items: ', which the' (A-03 D, B-04 D), ', so that' (A-04 D), ', that whatever' (A-05 C), ', and' / '. Then' (B-05 D/C), ', although' / ', whereupon' (A-06 C/D). Each strikes one distractor in A-03, A-04, A-05, A-06, B-04, B-05 — but B-06 keys the word-adding option ('whose') and A-06 keys a participle, so the rule does not choose the key.

Mark-family: semicolon keyed only where it is the lone semicolon (B-04); in A-03 and B-06 the semicolon is a distractor, so no consistent semicolon tell. Period is keyed in A-05 and wrong in A-03, A-06, B-05, B-06 — not reliable.

Subject-verb perfect items A-02 and B-01 both key the singular 'has + participle' against plural attractors; a student who learns 'pick singular has' wins both. With A-01 also keyed against attraction (plural this time), the batch is not uniformly singular.
Key letters are A,B,C,D x3 each — no letter tell.
near_duplicates: SEC14A-02 / SEC14B-01: same template — long subject with plural attractors, options {nonfinite or past-progressive, have+pp, has+pp}, key 'has + pp'.
SEC14A-03 / SEC14B-04: same option frame — {colon or comma, semicolon, period, ', which the'} at a clause boundary.
SEC14A-05 / SEC14B-04: both splice tests where the second clause's verb is far from the blank (looser).
